metaDescription: Six Greenworks 40V, 60V and 80V cordless snow blowers compared by voltage platform, clearing width and battery, so you buy the right tier.
expertTake: The 80V 20-inch kit is the strongest Greenworks for a real driveway, and the 40V 20-inch is the sensible pick if you already own 40V tools. The 40V 16-inch models are fine for walks and short drives. Nothing in this lineup replaces a two-stage gas machine on a long, heavily plowed drive. If you are choosing a platform from scratch, weigh the tool family you will add later as heavily as the blower.
introParagraphs: Few makers sell snow blowers across three separate battery platforms. That turns the shopping question into two decisions: which voltage system you already own, and which machine design fits the snow you actually get.

Most models in this range are single-stage designs with a rubber-tipped auger. They suit paved driveways and walks well, and the real differences lie in pack voltage, clearing width and whether a battery and charger come in the box.

products.name: Greenworks 80V 20-inch brushless snow blower, 4Ah kit
products.description:
This is the current 80V kit, a 20-inch single-stage with a brushless motor and a 4Ah pack plus fast charger. The 80V platform runs higher voltage than the 40V models, so the motor reaches its power with less current draw and less heat in the wiring.

Against the older 80V model with a 2Ah pack it ships with double the battery capacity, which is the difference between clearing a short drive and running out halfway. Against the 40V 20-inch it has the same path width but a bigger pack voltage, which should help hold power under load in thicker snow.

The usual battery-machine habits apply. Charge the pack before the forecast, keep it inside until the first pass and clear a jam with the pack removed. Since the 80V platform shares packs with Greenworks mowers and trimmers, owners with existing 80V tools can look at the cheaper tool-only versions. Plan on a second pack if your drive takes more than one charge, because the single 4Ah pack in the kit is the limiting factor rather than the motor. A spare pack also lets you rotate one on the charger while the other works.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want the strongest Greenworks single-stage for paved driveways.
pros: Higher 80V system keeps power under load
Brushless motor is quiet and low maintenance
cons: Only one battery in the kit limits runtime
Single-stage design struggles with heavy berms

products.name: Greenworks 60V 20-inch snow thrower, 4Ah kit
products.description:
The 60V thrower uses a 2.0 kilowatt brushless motor and a 4Ah pack that comes with a charger. The chute rotates 180 degrees and throws up to 25 feet, which is a shorter throw than some competing brands list but enough for typical walks.

It sits between the 40V and 80V lines, so its main appeal is to people already on the 60V tool platform. If you are not, the 80V kit is a better buy because it gets you a more current platform and a similar path width.

In use it behaves like the other single-stage Greenworks machines: it scrapes down to the pavement, struggles with berms and needs a patient second pass in heavy snow. Check the rubber paddles each season and keep the pack stored indoors. Before choosing it over the 80V kit, check whether you own any 60V mowers or trimmers; the savings from sharing a pack are the only strong argument for this middle platform.
products.bestFor: Owners already on the 60V Greenworks tool platform.
pros: 2.0 kW brushless motor with a 20-inch path
Pack and charger included in the kit
cons: Platform is less common than 40V or 80V

products.name: Greenworks 40V 20-inch snow blower, 5Ah kit
products.description:
The 40V 20-inch carries a brushless motor, a 10-inch clearing depth and a 5Ah pack in the kit. The throw is about 25 feet, so it covers a standard walk or short drive without much re-clearing.

The 5Ah pack is larger than the 4Ah on the 80V and 60V kits, but 40V packs store less energy per amp-hour than 80V ones, so do not assume the bigger number means more runtime. Compared with the 16-inch 40V models it clears a wider path, which means fewer passes.

Its biggest appeal is platform compatibility. Greenworks makes dozens of 40V tools, so a pack bought for the mower can run this machine. Store the pack indoors and keep the chute clear. If you already own a 40V pack from a mower or trimmer, the cheapest route may be a tool-only version of this machine, but check that the pack is at least 4Ah so the blower is not starved of runtime.
products.bestFor: Owners with a 40V Greenworks pack wanting the wider path.
cons: One pack limits runtime on larger drives
Less power headroom than the 80V platform

products.name: Greenworks 40V 16-inch Gen 2 snow blower, 5Ah kit
products.description:
The Gen 2 16-inch is a smaller, lighter 40V single-stage with a 10-inch clearing depth. The listing pairs it with a 5Ah pack and fast charger, so you can run it from the box.

The narrower 16-inch path means more passes per driveway than the 20-inch models, but the machine is easier to carry down basement stairs or store on a shelf. For narrow sidewalks and patios, a narrower footprint is actually an advantage.

Compared with the older SN40B410 below it is a refreshed model with a fast charger kit. The wear item is still the rubber paddle, so inspect it at the start of each season. A practical test before buying: measure your narrowest path and the clearance in your storage spot. If the 16-inch width is already wider than your walk, a 20-inch machine will only feel clumsy.
products.bestFor: Narrow walks, patios and small drives with limited storage.
pros: 10-inch snow depth in a compact body
Fast charger comes with the kit

products.name: Greenworks 40V 16-inch cordless snow blower SN40B410, 5Ah
products.description:
The SN40B410 uses a digitally controlled brushless motor and a handle that folds for storage. It is a proven earlier design and shares its 16-inch path and 40V pack with the Gen 2 model.

Its folding frame is the practical reason to choose it. In an apartment garage or a shed where every inch counts, a machine that collapses beats one that stands tall. Compared with the Gen 2 it lacks the newer kit, but it is otherwise similar.

Expect typical single-stage limitations. It works well in light to moderate snow, and a 5Ah pack is enough for a short drive. Do not leave the pack in a freezing garage. Folded, it stores upright against a wall without the handle sticking out, which matters more in an apartment garage than any spec on the sheet. The brushless motor keeps noise low enough for early-morning clearing.
products.bestFor: Small storage spaces where a folding handle is worth having.
cons: Older design than the Gen 2 model

products.name: Greenworks 40V 12-inch brushless snow shovel, 4Ah kit
products.description:
This 12-inch brushless snow shovel is the lightest tool in the Greenworks lineup. It is a better fit for steps, decks and short paths than for a full driveway.

Because it is a shovel, you carry the weight rather than wheel it. That keeps the unit light and the price modest, but it also limits how much snow you can move in a session. Its 4Ah pack and charger come in the kit.

Treat it as a companion to a larger machine. If your main need is a short walk and a small porch, it may be all you need.
pros: Very light and easy to maneuver
Easy to store on a hook

buyingCriteria.explanation: Greenworks sells 40V, 60V and 80V systems, and voltage alone does not determine runtime. The 80V 20-inch kit uses a 4Ah pack, the 40V 20-inch uses 5Ah, but 80V packs hold more energy per amp-hour. The mistake is buying a different platform when you already own another; shared packs save more than any spec difference. A good rule is to count the tools you own: three 80V tools in the garage make the 80V blower a bargain, while none make the platform choice free.

The 40V 20-inch clears 20 inches wide and 10 inches deep, while the 16-inch Gen 2 clears 16 by 10. Four inches of width means roughly one pass in five saved on a long run. For narrow walks the narrower body is easier to steer. Measure the narrowest point on your route before choosing; a path narrower than the machine forces awkward turning and extra passes.

Several Greenworks listings sell the machine without a battery or charger. A tool-only 40V 20-inch is only cheaper if you already own compatible packs. Count the cost of a pack and charger before comparing against a kit.

The 20-inch 40V and 60V models quote around 25 feet. That is enough for walks but may not clear snow past a plowed bank. Wind and wet snow will cut it further. Standing upwind of the chute and keeping the path clear of cars and fences avoids re-clearing the same snow twice.

Every full-size Greenworks here is a single-stage with a rubber-tipped auger. It scrapes pavement and throws snow in one step, so it is not built for deep berms, gravel or snow past about 10 inches. If your drive is gravel or heavily plowed, look at a two-stage instead. For snow deeper than about 10 inches, the machine has to lift and throw more than the rubber paddles can handle in one pass, so work in layers from the top down.

Lithium output drops sharply near 0 F. Store packs indoors, insert them just before use and avoid leaving them charging in an unheated garage. Two packs let one charge while the other works. A charger left in an unheated garage can refuse to start when the cell is too cold.

specDecoder.meaning: Removes carbon brushes, so there is less wear and heat. It also improves efficiency, which helps runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: All six picks here use brushless motors, so it does not separate them.

specDecoder.meaning: Amp-hours measure battery capacity at the pack voltage. Multiply by voltage for watt-hours. This is why a bigger number on a smaller voltage does not guarantee more runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: A 5Ah 40V pack holds about half the energy of a 5Ah 80V pack.

specDecoder.meaning: How deep a pass can go without bogging down.
The maximum range of the chute in light snow.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 60V and 40V 20-inch quote 25 feet; expect less in wet snow.

specDecoder.meaning: The machine ships without battery or charger.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some listings in this lineup omit the battery, so read what is in the box.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We grouped the lineup by 40V, 60V and 80V because platform lock-in is the biggest cost factor. We noted which kits include battery and charger. The 80V 20-inch kit and 40V 20-inch kit are compared on path width.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pack amp-hours and voltage together. A 4Ah 80V pack, a 4Ah 60V pack and a 5Ah 40V pack do not store the same energy. We used that to rank runtime potential. We also looked at which listings ship with the pack and which do not, because the missing battery is the most common surprise.

howWeEvaluated.title: Clearing geometry
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared widths of 12, 16 and 20 inches and clearing depths of 10 inches where listed. Wider paths save passes, narrower ones suit steps. We treated the quoted 25-foot throw as a best-case figure in light snow.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed paddle wear, pack storage and cold-weather charging. A brushless battery machine avoids gas and carburetor work but adds pack care. Pack care is the ownership cost that replaces fuel and spark plugs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Honest fit
howWeEvaluated.description: Every model is a single-stage or shovel, so we rated none against deep berm or gravel jobs. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. That means the 12-inch shovel, 16-inch Gen 2 and 20-inch kits are judged against the jobs they are designed for.

rows: Wider path on the common platform

cards.label: 40V
cards.text: The 40V models such as the 20-inch 5Ah kit share batteries with the broadest set of Greenworks tools. They are the practical choice for most owners.

cards.label: 80V
cards.text: The 80V 20-inch kit uses a higher-voltage platform that holds power better under load. It makes sense if you already own other 80V tools or want the strongest option.

howToChoose.note: Choose 40V if you already own those tools; choose 80V if you are starting fresh and have a longer drive.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A folding handle and a light body, so the machine hangs on a wall or fits a shelf. Check the folded dimensions before you buy.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Greenworks SN40B410 folds for storage and the 12-inch shovel hangs on a hook. Both suit tight garages.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your drive is long or you own other 80V tools. The 80V 20-inch kit is the strongest in this lineup.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only clear a walk and steps. The 40V 12-inch shovel or 16-inch Gen 2 will do the job.

maintenance.why: A half-charged pack stalls mid-drive. Charge indoors so the pack starts warm.
Paddles wear with every pass. Replace them when the edge no longer scrapes. Also check the scraper bar for cracks, because a bent bar leaves a strip of ice behind.

maintenance.task: Wipe the chute and auger housing
maintenance.why: Slush freezes overnight. A wipe keeps the chute free.
Lithium cells age faster when stored full or empty. Keep them cool and dry. Avoid a hot garage or a freezing shed; an interior closet is better than either.
A jammed auger can restart suddenly. Never use hands.

faq.q: Which Greenworks voltage should I choose?
faq.a: Match the platform you already own. If you are starting fresh, the 80V 20-inch kit is the strongest here, while 40V has the widest tool family. Owning three or more tools on one platform tips the answer toward that platform even when another machine looks slightly better on paper.
No. Single-stage rubber augers throw loose stones. Use a two-stage with raised skid shoes on gravel. A bare tool with the wrong cable or charger is a common first-winter frustration.

faq.q: Does a larger Ah number mean more runtime?
faq.a: Only when voltage is the same. A 5Ah 40V pack holds less energy than a 4Ah 80V pack.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last in a storm?
faq.a: It depends on snow depth and wetness. Makers quote times from light snow; plan for less in heavy snow and keep a second pack handy. A spare pack on the charger keeps you working through a long clear.

faq.q: Are the tool-only models worth it?
faq.a: Only if you already own compatible packs and a charger. Otherwise a kit costs less than buying parts separately.
For steps, decks and a short walk, yes. For a driveway, step up to the 16-inch or 20-inch machines.
